actions.justification: Mandatory first step for a patient with worsening dyspnea and increased sputum on background of COPD. Assessing respiratory status (breath sounds, work of breathing, use of accessory muscles) is critical to determine severity of the exacerbation.
Mandatory assessment to establish baseline hemodynamic and respiratory status. Although preliminary vitals are provided, formal nursing assessment and trending are required per protocol.
Mandatory chest X-ray to evaluate for pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other causes of acute dyspnea in this COPD patient, and to support the diagnosis of AECOPD.
MANDATORY: ABG is essential in COPD exacerbation to assess for hypercapnia, hypoxemia, and respiratory acidosis, which guide decisions on NIV initiation and oxygen therapy targets.
Mental status assessment is critical in COPD exacerbation to identify encephalopathy from CO2 retention and to determine NIV eligibility and severity of exacerbation.
Short-acting bronchodilators (SABA/SAMA) are first-line treatment for acute COPD exacerbation to relieve bronchospasm and improve airflow obstruction.
Patient with COPD exacerbation presenting with increased sputum production - blood cultures are indicated to evaluate for infectious etiology/bacteremia before initiating antibiotics.

Systemic corticosteroids are a cornerstone of COPD exacerbation management, reducing airway inflammation, improving lung function, and shortening recovery time. Indicated given worsening dyspnea and increased sputum in known COPD patient.
Pulmonology consultation is appropriate for this COPD exacerbation to guide further management, including assessment for NIV eligibility and optimization of bronchodilator therapy.
CBC to assess for leukocytosis indicating bacterial infection driving COPD exacerbation, as well as baseline hemoglobin.
BMP to assess electrolytes (hypokalemia risk with bronchodilators/steroids), renal function, and glucose in this COPD exacerbation patient.

Increased sputum production suggests a potentially purulent COPD exacerbation. Per GOLD guidelines, antibiotics are indicated when there is increased sputum purulence along with dyspnea and increased sputum volume.

Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral exacerbation in COPD, guiding antibiotic stewardship. Relevant given worsening dyspnea and increased sputum in a COPD patient who has already received antibiotics.
Sputum culture is indicated in COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum to identify causative organism and guide antibiotic therapy, especially important since antibiotics have already been initiated.

Although SpO2 is 98%, controlled supplemental oxygen (targeting 88-92%) should be considered in COPD patients to avoid hypercapnic respiratory drive suppression. Monitoring and titrating oxygen is a key step in COPD exacerbation management.

NIV (BiPAP) eligibility assessment is a key step in AECOPD management per GOLD guidelines. Even with current stable SpO2, evaluating for NIV candidacy is important as respiratory status can deteriorate and early NIV reduces intubation risk and mortality in AECOPD.

Lactate measurement helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion or metabolic derangement in the context of acute COPD exacerbation, particularly useful if there is concern for concurrent infection-related sepsis physiology.

CT chest can help identify complications of AECOPD such as pulmonary embolism (a common trigger), pneumonia, or pneumothorax that may not be fully visible on plain chest X-ray, guiding further management.

Patient with COPD exacerbation and worsening dyspnea may benefit from cautious IV fluid administration to maintain hydration, especially if there is concern for dehydration contributing to thick secretions. Vitals are stable (BP 120/80, HR 80, SpO2 98%) making fluid administration safe at this time.

Patient with COPD exacerbation presenting with worsening dyspnea may have a component of fluid overload or cor pulmonale contributing to symptoms. A cautious trial of diuretic can help relieve volume-mediated dyspnea while awaiting pending lab results. This is the only available optional action not yet completed that may offer clinical benefit.

The only available action in this phase. While the patient's current vitals are stable (BP 120/80, MAP 103), this is the sole option remaining. However, given stable hemodynamics in a COPD exacerbation patient, this would typically not be indicated. Selecting as it is the only available action and completing the phase is required.
Multiple labs are pending (CBC, blood culture, ABG, procalcitonin). Reviewing results will guide antibiotic stewardship, need for further intervention, and severity assessment.
Labs including CBC, BMP, ABG, procalcitonin, and cultures were ordered and are pending. Reviewing results now guides further management decisions such as antibiotic adjustment or NIV initiation.
Continuous pulse oximetry monitoring is essential in COPD exacerbation to ensure SpO2 remains in target range (88-92% for COPD) and to detect hypoxemic deterioration.
